processing: Anhua dark raw tea (hei mao cha), made with fixing, rolling, pile fermentation and pine-fire drying, then graded and refined. San Jian is the loose family of this tea, not pressed like Anhua's bricks.
harvest_season: Grade depends on the leaf: Tian Jian uses the best raw tea, then Gong Jian, then Sheng Jian. As usual for Anhua dark tea, the finer leaf comes from the earlier pickings.
appearance_dry: Dark, glossy twisted leaf in Tian Jian, coarser and browner in the lower grades.
appearance_wet: Yellow-brown to dark brown whole and broken leaf.
taste_profile: Tian Jian is full and rich, with the mellow body and light pine smoke typical of Anhua dark tea. The lower grades are plainer and lighter.

brewing.notes: Rinse quickly. Boiling water in a pot or gaiwan; long steeps bring out more smoke and grip.

vintage_note: Sold by grade and production year, as with other Anhua dark teas, and drunk both within a few years and aged. Older tea should smell clean, with the smoke softened. Always check which of the three grades you are buying, since San Jian alone does not say.
description:
San Jian, the three tips, is the loose branch of Anhua dark tea: Tian Jian, Gong Jian and Sheng Jian, from highest grade to lowest. Together with three bricks and one roll, they make up the classic set of Anhua teas. You may also see them called Xiang Jian.

All three begin as hei mao cha, the region's raw dark tea, with pile fermentation and drying over a pine fire. The difference lies mainly in the grade of leaf used, and that is why the same family runs from a rich, dark tea to a simple everyday one.

The cup is orange-yellow and clear, with a light pine smoke over a rounded body, typical of Anhua. Tian Jian is the one with real depth. Brew all three with boiling water, and shorten the steeps if the smoke takes over.

When buying, go by named grade, maker and year. Baishaxi is the factory most tied to the revival of these teas. If you want the smokier, more rustic side of dark tea without breaking a brick, this is the easy way in.
history:
Tip teas are said to have been made in Anhua by the Qianlong period. According to Hunan press accounts, the Daoguang Emperor gave Tian Jian its name and made it a palace tea, with Gong Jian and Sheng Jian going as gifts to the nobility; treat that story with some care.

The Baishaxi factory, founded in 1939, helped revive and continue the family. In 1967, during the Cultural Revolution, it renamed the three teas Xiang Jian Nos. 1, 2 and 3, and the old names came back in 1983.
